title: THE MOST DANGEROUS BETRAYAL BEGINS WITH SOMEONE WHO MAKES YOU FEEL UNDERSTOOD
paragraphs: THE MOST DANGEROUS BETRAYAL BEGINS WITH SOMEONE WHO MAKES YOU FEEL UNDERSTOOD
Why Absalom Stood at the City Gate to Steal Hearts—and the Terrifying Difference Between Someone Who Cares About Your Pain and Someone Who Wants to Use It
He didn't begin by attacking the throne. He began by listening to wounded people.
And that is what made him so dangerous.
Imagine walking into a city carrying a burden nobody seems to care about.

You have been wronged. You have waited for justice. You have rehearsed what you would say if someone in authority would finally listen. But the doors seem closed, the powerful seem distant, and your pain feels invisible.
Then one morning, someone approaches you.
He doesn't look down on you. He doesn't dismiss your complaint. He asks where you are from. He listens to your story. He tells you that your concerns are legitimate.
Then he says something you have desperately wanted to hear.
"If only I were the one in charge, things would be different."
You feel seen.
You feel valued.
For the first time in a long time, you feel that somebody understands.
And without realizing it, your heart begins moving toward a man whose compassion may not be compassion at all.
His name was Absalom.
He was the son of King David.
And the Bible records one of the most chilling descriptions of political manipulation ever written:
"So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel." — 2 Samuel 15:6, KJV
Not their money.
Not their property.
Not their weapons.
Their hearts.
And before we examine what happened at that ancient city gate, there is a question we cannot afford to avoid.
What if the person who makes you feel most understood is also the person quietly leading you away from what is right?
Because Absalom's story is not merely about a rebellious prince thousands of years ago.
It is about the vulnerability of the human heart.
It is about what happens when genuine wounds meet calculated ambition.
And it is about why we desperately need a Savior who does not exploit our brokenness but redeems it.
Absalom was not an ordinary man.
He was handsome, admired, royal, and influential. Second Samuel 14:25 describes his extraordinary physical appearance, saying that throughout Israel there was no one praised as highly for his beauty.
He had the appearance of someone born to lead.
But beneath that impressive exterior was a deeply troubled family history.

His sister Tamar had been sexually violated by their half-brother Amnon. David became angry when he heard what had happened, but the biblical narrative records no corresponding punishment of Amnon. Absalom carried hatred toward Amnon for two years before arranging his murder.
The tragedy is recorded in 2 Samuel 13.
This matters because Absalom's later rebellion did not emerge from nowhere.
His family had experienced terrible injustice, moral failure, silence, vengeance, estrangement, and unresolved conflict.

Absalom fled after Amnon's death. Eventually he returned to Jerusalem, but for two years he was not permitted to see his father's face. Even after their eventual reunion, Scripture does not describe a deep restoration of their relationship.
We should be careful not to pretend the Bible tells us every private thought Absalom had.
It doesn't.
But it does show us a man shaped by a painful history who would eventually use other people's grievances to build his own power.
And that distinction is devastating.
You can have a legitimate wound and still choose an unrighteous response.
You can be genuinely mistreated and later mistreat others.
You can recognize corruption in someone else's life while refusing to confront the corruption growing inside your own heart.
Pain may explain how bitterness develops.
It does not make betrayal righteous.
Then came the city gate.
Second Samuel 15:1 tells us that Absalom prepared a chariot, horses, and fifty men to run before him.
This was not simply transportation.
It was a public display of status.
He was presenting himself as someone important, someone with royal presence, someone worth noticing.
Then verse 2 tells us that Absalom rose early and stood beside the road leading to the city gate.
That detail is easy to overlook.
He rose early.
He positioned himself deliberately.
And he chose a location where people seeking judgment would pass.

In ancient Israel, the city gate was far more than an entrance through a wall. It was a significant public gathering place where legal disputes, transactions, and community affairs could be addressed. Passages such as Ruth 4:1–11 and Deuteronomy 21:18–21 help us understand this setting.
Absalom was not standing in a random location hoping to meet interesting people.
He was placing himself where people came carrying unresolved disputes.
Where frustration gathered.
Where disappointment could be found.
Where the desire for justice made people especially receptive to anyone promising to provide it.
He understood something that remains painfully relevant.
If you want to influence a wounded person, first convince that person you understand the wound.
Second Samuel 15:2–3 describes his approach.
He would call out to someone who had come seeking the king's judgment, ask what city the person came from, and hear about the person's case.
Then he would respond:
"See, thy matters are good and right; but there is no man deputed of the king to hear thee." — 2 Samuel 15:3, KJV
Think about what he was doing.
He affirmed the person's position.
He suggested the royal administration was failing them.
And he presented himself as someone who recognized what others had neglected.
Notice that the narrative does not say Absalom carefully investigated each case before declaring it good and right.
His repeated affirmation served his larger campaign.
He was not merely comforting people.
He was cultivating their loyalty.
And that should make us examine some of the voices we allow to influence us.
Not everyone who agrees with your anger is helping you heal.
Not everyone who validates your feelings is telling you the truth.
Not everyone who condemns your enemies has your best interests at heart.
Sometimes the person who always tells you that you are right is not protecting you.
Sometimes that person is protecting their access to you.
And sometimes the most loving voice in your life is the one courageous enough to tell you something you do not want to hear.
Proverbs 27:6 says:
"Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful." — KJV
Read that again.
A faithful friend may wound your pride by speaking truth.
An enemy may soothe your pride while leading you toward destruction.
Absalom understood the persuasive power of making people feel justified.
But he went further.
He said:
"Oh that I were made judge in the land, that every man which hath any suit or cause might come unto me, and I would do him justice!" — 2 Samuel 15:4, KJV
There it was.
The promise.
If only I had authority.
If only I were in charge.
If only you would trust me.
Everything would be better.
He presented himself as the answer to problems he was using to gain influence.
He was not yet openly declaring war against his father in that moment.
He was quietly building the emotional foundation for rebellion.
And he was doing it one conversation at a time.
Then Scripture reveals another disturbing detail.
When someone approached to bow before him, Absalom would extend his hand, take hold of the person, and kiss him.
In the social world of ancient Israel, such gestures could communicate affection, welcome, and personal regard.
For a royal prince to offer that kind of attention could make an ordinary person feel remarkably important.
Imagine the contrast.
A person arrives feeling overlooked by the royal system.
Then the king's own son personally greets him with warmth.
The experience could be unforgettable.
But the biblical narrator does not leave us guessing about the larger result.
Absalom was stealing hearts.
There is a striking expression in the Hebrew text of 2 Samuel 15:6:
וַיְגַנֵּב אַבְשָׁלוֹם אֶת־לֵב אַנְשֵׁי יִשְׂרָאֵל
Vayegannev Avshalom et-lev anshei Yisra'el.
A close rendering is:
"And Absalom stole the heart of the men of Israel."
The verb וַיְגַנֵּב (vayegannev) comes from the Hebrew root גנב (g-n-b), meaning "to steal."
The word לֵב (lev) means "heart," but in biblical Hebrew the heart is not merely the seat of emotion. It can also encompass thought, intention, desire, and decision.
So the description is deeper than Absalom simply making people like him.
He was gaining their allegiance.
He was redirecting their loyalties.
He was drawing their inner commitment toward himself.
This is not an invented spiritual meaning hidden inside the Hebrew. It is the force of the narrative itself.
Absalom was deliberately winning the people over, and the biblical writer chose the language of theft to describe what he accomplished.
That is the terrible irony.
He promised justice while pursuing a throne through deception.
He presented himself as a servant of the people while building a movement around himself.
He offered gestures of affection while preparing an act of betrayal.
And eventually, the consequences would be catastrophic.
Second Samuel 15:10–12 describes Absalom's conspiracy advancing. He sent messengers throughout the tribes, arranged for his kingship to be proclaimed, and drew more people into his cause.
By verse 13, a messenger came to David with alarming news:
"The hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom." — 2 Samuel 15:13, KJV
The strategy had worked.
The conversations at the gate had become a national crisis.
The wounded king would soon flee Jerusalem.
The royal household would be thrown into turmoil.
And Israel would suffer through a devastating rebellion.
What began with flattering words became a tragedy of bloodshed and grief.
That is how dangerous unchecked ambition can become.
It rarely announces its full intentions at the beginning.
It may first arrive as concern.
As agreement.
As sympathy.
As the comforting promise that someone finally understands.
But Scripture calls us to discernment, not paranoia.

We must not assume that every compassionate person is manipulative. Genuine listening is a gift. Caring for people who have been neglected is righteous. Seeking justice for the oppressed is a biblical responsibility.
Absalom's sin was not that he listened.
His sin was that he used listening as a weapon for self-exaltation and rebellion.
And there is an important warning here for anyone entrusted with influence.
Pastors.
Ministry leaders.
Parents.
Teachers.
Employers.
Public servants.
Christian content creators.
Even those of us who simply have someone's confidence.
When people come to us hurting, their vulnerability is not an opportunity to make ourselves indispensable.
Their trust is not something to exploit.
Their pain is not a platform on which to build our own importance.
The call of Christ is not to make wounded people dependent on our personalities.
It is to love them truthfully and direct them toward God.
John the Baptist expressed the heart of faithful ministry when he said of Jesus:
"He must increase, but I must decrease." — John 3:30, KJV
Absalom's ambition said, in effect, "If only I were made judge."
John's humility said, "He must increase."
Two radically different ways of handling influence.
One uses people to rise.
The other points people to the One who is worthy.
And perhaps this is where the story becomes uncomfortably personal.
Have you ever wanted people to recognize how badly someone treated you?
Have you ever replayed a painful conversation, imagining the day everyone would finally see that you were right?
Have you ever found yourself enjoying the attention of someone who constantly confirmed your grievances?
Have you ever been tempted to gather people to your side instead of pursuing truth, reconciliation, and righteousness?
Or perhaps you have been on the other side.
Perhaps someone earned your trust by listening to your pain, only to turn your vulnerability into leverage.
Perhaps you defended someone because they made you feel special.
Perhaps you ignored warning signs because their attention felt like healing.
And when everything fell apart, you wondered how you could have trusted them.
The Bible does not tell you to become hardhearted because people can be deceptive.
It calls you to become discerning.
And it invites you to bring your wounds to someone who will never need to manipulate you to accomplish His purposes.
Jesus Christ.
Here is where the contrast becomes extraordinary.
Absalom stood beside the road to the city gate, positioning himself to win the loyalty of people seeking justice.
Jesus came into a broken world proclaiming the kingdom of God, calling sinners to repentance, welcoming the weary, and bringing salvation through His death and resurrection.
Absalom wanted the throne.
Jesus already possessed divine glory, yet willingly humbled Himself.
Philippians 2:6–8 teaches that Christ, though truly divine, took the form of a servant and humbled Himself in obedience unto death, even death on a cross.
Absalom used affection to advance himself.
Jesus demonstrated love by giving Himself.
Absalom promised to make things right if he received power.
Jesus gave His life to reconcile sinners to God.
Absalom's rebellion brought suffering to his father's kingdom.
Jesus, the promised Son of David, suffered to establish the salvation of His people.
These are theological contrasts drawn from the larger witness of Scripture, not a claim that every detail of Absalom's actions was written as a direct prophecy about Christ.
But the contrast is unmistakable.
Absalom wanted people's hearts so he could become king. Jesus is the rightful King who gave His life to redeem people's hearts.
And there is another scene we must not overlook.
After Absalom's rebellion ended, David heard that his son had died.
His response was not a triumphant celebration over a defeated enemy.
It was the cry of a grieving father.
"O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son!" — 2 Samuel 18:33, KJV
Can you hear the anguish?
The son who had stolen hearts.
The son who had betrayed his father.
The son whose ambition had torn a kingdom apart.
Now dead.
And David wept.
There is something heartbreaking about a father wishing he could have died instead of his rebellious son.
But David could not undo Absalom's death.
He could not reverse the destruction.
He could not save his son by grieving.
And this is where the Gospel shines with a glory greater than the tragedy.
David cried out with the wish that he could have died in his son's place.
Jesus Christ actually gave His life for sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." — KJV
Not because we had earned His affection.
Not because we had never rebelled.
Not because our motives were always pure.
But because of God's astonishing grace.
And unlike Absalom, whose death marked the defeat of his rebellion, Jesus rose from the dead in victory over sin and death.
The resurrection is not an emotional footnote.
It is central to the Christian hope.
Christ was crucified for our sins, buried, and raised on the third day, according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
The King who saves is alive.
And He does not merely promise to understand your suffering.
He calls you into a new life.
A life of repentance.
A life of forgiveness.
A life of truth.
A life where the wounds of yesterday do not have to become the weapons of tomorrow.
Maybe that is the word you needed today.
You have been hurt.
Deeply.
Someone failed you.
Someone betrayed you.
Someone should have protected you and didn't.
Someone in authority should have acted justly and remained silent.
And perhaps you have been standing at your own invisible city gate, waiting for someone to tell you that your pain matters.
It does.
God is not indifferent to injustice.
But please hear this.
Do not let the person who hurt you determine the person you become.
Do not let bitterness write the ending of your story.
Do not confuse revenge with healing.
Do not surrender your conscience to someone simply because they validate your anger.
And do not imagine that following Jesus means pretending evil never happened.
Biblical forgiveness does not require calling wickedness good, abandoning wise boundaries, or shielding abusers from appropriate accountability.
Jesus calls us into truth as well as grace.
Repentance does not erase the need for justice.
And healing does not require denying the wound.
It means allowing Christ to transform what sin and suffering have threatened to destroy.
Perhaps your greatest danger today is not an Absalom standing outside your door.
Perhaps it is an Absalom-like desire growing quietly within you.
The hunger to be admired.
The need to be vindicated.
The temptation to manipulate sympathy.
The willingness to say whatever people want to hear because you are afraid of losing their approval.
If that truth stings, do not run from it.
Bring it to Jesus.
The Gospel is not only for people who have been betrayed.
It is also for people who must repent of betraying others.
It is for the wounded and the guilty.
For the proud and the ashamed.
For the person whose heart was stolen and the person who has tried to steal hearts for selfish gain.
There is mercy in Christ for sinners who turn to Him in genuine repentance and faith.
First John 1:9 says:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." — KJV
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That is not permission to continue in sin.
It is an invitation to leave sin behind and walk in the light.
And perhaps right now, the most courageous prayer you could pray is not, "Lord, expose everyone who wronged me."
Perhaps it is:
"Lord, search my heart too."
Because it is possible to be right about another person's wrongdoing and still be wrong in how we respond.
It is possible to seek justice without surrendering to vengeance.
It is possible to tell the truth without becoming cruel.
It is possible to remember the past without allowing the past to rule the future.
And through Jesus Christ, it is possible to begin again.
If this message has uncovered something you have been carrying, you do not have to pretend you are fine.
You can pray right where you are.

"Lord Jesus, You know the wounds I have hidden, the anger I have justified, and the places where pride has influenced my decisions. Forgive my sins. Teach me to love truth more than applause, righteousness more than revenge, and Your glory more than my own recognition. Heal what is broken, correct what is sinful, and help me walk in repentance and faith. Guard my heart from deception, and keep me from using other people's pain for selfish purposes. Thank You for dying for sinners and rising again. Lead me in Your ways. Amen."
And if that prayer reflects something happening in your heart, consider leaving a comment.
You can simply write, "Lord, guard my heart."
You do not need to disclose private details or expose your deepest wounds publicly. Sometimes a few honest words are enough to remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
And if you have experienced God's grace after a season of bitterness, betrayal, or spiritual confusion, your testimony may encourage someone who is still finding the courage to turn back to Christ.
Because the message of Absalom is not merely that people can deceive us.
It is that our hearts must belong to someone greater than the people who flatter us, disappoint us, or promise to rescue us.
They must belong to Jesus.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to gather hearts around a personality.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to make anyone dependent on a ministry brand.
But to point people continually to the Lord Jesus Christ through Scripture, Gospel-centered encouragement, repentance, discipleship, and the truth that transforms lives.
Not because these words are more important than Scripture, but because there may come a day when you need to remember the lesson of the city gate.
The voice that makes you feel understood is not always the voice that leads you toward truth.
And for those who want to go deeper, there is another way to help this work continue.
These resources are offered freely because biblical nourishment should not be reserved only for people who can afford to pay.
But making resources available, preparing Scripture-centered content, maintaining ministry outreach, and expanding the work all require ongoing support.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving must come from a willing heart.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — KJV
That is the spirit in which we ask for support.
Not guilt.
Not spiritual pressure.
Not a promise that giving money will purchase God's favor.
But a shared desire to make Christ known.
The Gospel is not for sale.
We give because Christ has first given Himself for us.
We serve because He first loved us.
We share because the truth of His Gospel is too precious to keep to ourselves.
And we support faithful ministry because we want more people to know the Savior who changes lives.
Picture Absalom standing there.
The chariot.
The horses.
The fifty men.
The impressive appearance.
The carefully chosen words.
The warm embrace.
The promise of justice.
The growing crowd.
Everything looked so convincing.
But beneath the surface, hearts were being drawn toward a rebellion that would end in tears.
And then picture another scene.
Not a prince displaying his importance.
But Jesus Christ, crowned with thorns.
Not fifty men running before Him to announce His greatness.
But soldiers mocking Him.
Not a man promising to serve if he could gain a throne.
But the rightful King giving His life to save sinners.
One sought power through the loyalty of others.
The other revealed divine love through sacrificial obedience.
And the question that remains is not merely whether you can recognize another person's manipulation.
It is whether you have surrendered your own heart to Jesus Christ.
Who has your loyalty?
Whose approval governs your decisions?
Whose voice has become more important than God's Word?
And when your pain speaks loudly, will you allow bitterness to lead you, or will you bring that pain into the light of Christ?
Absalom's story warns us that a heart can be won by the wrong person.
The Gospel announces that a sinful heart can be redeemed by the right Savior.
The King who died and rose again still calls people to repent, believe, and follow Him.
So do not give your soul to the loudest promise.
Do not give your future to the deepest resentment.
Do not let a counterfeit rescuer take the place of Christ.
Give your heart to the One who is worthy of it.
And remember this:
Absalom stood at the gate to steal hearts. Jesus went to the cross to redeem them.
